meaningNote: The Trust exists to support monasteries worldwide: donors give to it, and it passes the money on to the trust or foundation that looks after the monastery they want to help. The Trust runs no monastery and has no staff. Its spending is money passed on to monasteries, which then appears in their own accounts as money in, so it must not be added to their costs.
holdNote: Almost all of it is restricted: given for a named monastery, so it cannot be used for anything else. At the end of 2024 about £146,951 was held for Sumedharama's trust and £48,220 for Pannagiri; unrestricted funds were £4,575, and at the end of 2025 a deficit of £5,010 because of unpaid audit fees.
notes: What this is. The Theravada Monastic Trust (charity 1127588, company 6762469, registered 2009) is a charity in England that takes donations from people who want to support the monasteries and passes them on as grants. It runs no monastery, has no employees and owns no property, only cash held until it is passed on. Its objects are to support residential monasteries for a monastic sangha and lay practice. It is on this page because money moves between the monasteries and this Trust, which the monasteries' own accounts do not show.

Why it exists, in its own words. The Charity Commission register describes it this way: "The main object of the charity is to support the development of a Theravada Buddhist Monastic Sangha worldwide. The Charity supports visits by monastics, retreats and the development of infrastructures for monasteries." Its legal objects are to promote the teachings of the Buddha by providing, maintaining and supporting residential establishments for a monastic sangha, and by supporting lay people in the practice. The register shows its earlier name as the Portuguese Theravada Buddhist Monastic Trust, and lists Italy, Portugal, the United States and Hertfordshire as where it works. In its accounts the trustees say donors "generally wish to support the development and ongoing costs of the upkeep of the monasteries", that it is run entirely by volunteers, and that its reserves policy is to pass money on to whichever stewardship trust or foundation the donors are supporting, as long as it is a viable concern. It does not build up reserves, because it provides no services of its own.

What happened, year by year. The Trust began in 2009 as the Portuguese Theravada Buddhist Monastic Trust, a UK charity that lets supporters in Britain give to the monastery being built in Portugal (Sumedharama) with Gift Aid. Over the years it widened to other monasteries. Money comes in as donations (each one marked for a named monastery), waits in a fund for that monastery, and is passed on as a grant when the monastery's own trust asks for it. The figures below are from the Trust's accounts; the grants are as the accounts name them. Amounts in pounds.

Altogether, 2020 to 2025: £3,312,887 came in and £3,238,938 went out. About £2.0 million of it is the 2025 gift and about £1.0 million is the 2024 Pannagiri purchase; the other four years together came to about £0.17 million in and £0.25 million out. The Trust has no employees, and its own running costs are small (£434 in 2024, £13,195 of governance costs in 2025, which includes the audit).

Where the figures come from. The Trust's annual accounts to the Charity Commission, via opencharities.uk (opencharities_1127588.json in this folder keeps the register data, without contact details): total income, total expenditure and money held for the years to 31 December 2020 to 2025. One correction: for 2023 the register data show £156,294 as spending, which is the money held at the end of that year; the accounts show £22,077 spent, which is used here. The accounts for 2021, 2023, 2024 and 2025 were read for the grants and what they were for. The 2020 and 2022 accounts could not be opened, so those years come from the comparison columns of the next year's accounts. Where the accounts' tables were unclear (for example how the £11,252 for Sumedharama in 2021 was classed), the page says what is shown. For 2025 the register gives income of £2,023,772; the accounts' own statement may differ by about £500.

Do not add these to the monasteries' costs. A grant paid by the Trust shows up as money in for the monastery that receives it, and only becomes a cost when the monastery spends it. Adding the Trust's spending to the monasteries' would count the same money twice. Two of the Trust's trustees also serve on the bodies that received the larger English grants, as the Trust's accounts say.

Spending is total spending. The accounts show no running costs, no building work and no wear on buildings, so this page shows no running cost and no change after inflation. Years before 2020 are not in the register data used here.
Residents. There are none: the Trust is not a monastery.
